newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesians warned against religious provocation.
newsitem.headline: Indonesians warned against religious provocation.

text.p: Indonesia's top Islamic body on Monday warned citizens of all faiths to be on guard against religious provocation after at least five people died in a spate of church burnings in East Java last week.

The message came after the Nahdlatul Ulama (NU), Indonesia's largest Moslem group, apologised and asked for forgiveness for an attack by thousands of Moslems on churches around Situbondo in East Java on Thursday.

The government has said five were killed, but a statement from the Communion of Churches in Indonesia said six people had died including a pastor, his wife, two children and a maid. It said one other person was killed but did not give details.
The statement said 25 churches were burned or damaged in the attacks, which the Jakarta Post newspaper said involved around 10,000 people. Police have said only nine churches were set on fire.

Hasan Basri, chairman of the official Indonesian Ulama Council (MUI), said in a statement it regretted the disturbance and said the Prophet had forbidden Moslems to destroy places of worship or religious people.

"The MUI urges all believers, especially Moslems, to watch out for the possibility that they could be used by irresponsible parties to incite conflict between religions, Moslems themselves as well as Moslems and the government, in an effort to fracture national unity," he said.

Abdurrahman Wahid, leader of the 30-million-strong NU, said in a statement that the rioting in the town of Situbondo was most likely carried out by his members as the province is in the group's heartland.
"Those who carried out the 'Situbondo Incident' were generally NU members and this incident becomes the moral responsibilty of the national NU leadership, including myself as chairman," Wahid said.
"I, as head, apologise for the losses which are suffered by the government and community and express my deep condolences to the victims who died and were injured," Wahid said.
"I ask for God to forgive those who did this thing without knowing the serious consequences for the community, nation and state," he said.
The riot broke out after a court hearing into a case of alleged blasphemy against Islam in Situbondo, about 160 km (100 miles) east of Indonesia's second-largest city, Surabaya.

Several thousand people outside the court during the third hearing of the case called for the accused, a Moslem identified as Mohamad Saleh, to be sentenced immediately or be handed over to the crowd.

The Media Indonesia daily on Monday quoted the Situbondo chief judge, who sustained a head wound when hit by a stone during the riot, as saying he had postponed the sentencing of Saleh, due on Monday, because the court had been destroyed.
The incident was the latest in a series of attacks on Christian establishments, blamed by religious scholars on economic pressure and deep-seated religious rivalries.
A hall used by Catholics for worship in East Jakarta was burned down last month. A number of churches were burned in the Surabaya area in June.
